defaults.teacher_persona: A risk and compliance lead who turns frameworks into decisions a small organisation can actually run, and who says plainly when a question needs counsel.
classmates: An operations manager who has no compliance team
A works-council-style employee representative focused on monitoring and dignity
defaults.interaction: Case review: the teacher walks one scenario through the framework, then the peers apply it to a scenario of their own and defend the residual risk.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: Frameworks That Apply to Your Organisation
classrooms.prompt: Introduce the main governance reference points at a working level: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's functions, the OECD principles, and the risk-based structure of the EU AI Act, with the class noting that obligations and dates vary and must be checked rather than assumed. The teacher maps one use case (AI-assisted hiring screening) onto govern-map-measure-manage, then the peers map a use case of their own. Include slides on what each framework is for and is not, a roleplay where a sales team asks whether the product is 'compliant', and a quiz on which statement is safe to make publicly.
objectives: Name the purpose of the main AI governance frameworks
Map a use case onto the NIST functions
Avoid making compliance claims that cannot be supported

classrooms.title: Risk Assessment You Can Defend
classrooms.prompt: Run a risk assessment on a supplied use case: affected people, harms (including harms of denial or error, not only privacy), likelihood, severity, existing controls, residual risk, and the owner who accepts it. The teacher shows a register entry that hides an unmitigated harm behind an average score, and the peers rewrite it. Include slides on risk statements versus adjectives, a roleplay where a sponsor wants the register entry softened, and a quiz on which residual-risk decision needs escalation. Emphasise that accepting risk is a named person's decision, recorded.
objectives: Write a risk statement with affected people and harm
Record controls and residual risk honestly
Escalate a risk above your authority

activities.title: A register entry that survives review

classrooms.title: Transparency, Disclosure, and Worker Rights
classrooms.prompt: Work through disclosure and monitoring: when people must be told AI is in use, what a useful notice says, how automated decisions should be explained, and where monitoring crosses into surveillance. The teacher compares a vague notice with a specific one, then the peers draft a notice for a use case where AI scores job applicants. Include slides on notice and explanation, a roleplay where a manager wants to monitor productivity silently, and a quiz on which practice needs a formal decision. Note that legal requirements vary by jurisdiction and sector and must be confirmed.
objectives: Write a notice that says what the AI does and does not decide
Explain an automated decision in plain language
Recognise monitoring that needs a formal decision

classrooms.title: Vendor Review and Incident Response
classrooms.prompt: Run a vendor review of an AI feature: data categories, training use, retention, subprocessors and location, security evidence, accuracy and evaluation claims, human oversight, exit and deletion, and liability. The teacher shows two answers to the same question (one specific, one evasive) and how to score them, then the peers review a supplied vendor pack and list the three questions that decide the deal. Include a short incident drill: an AI feature gives a wrong answer to a customer and it is on social media. Close with the first-hour incident checklist.
objectives: Evaluate vendor answers on data use and retention
Score accuracy claims by their evidence
Run the first hour of an AI incident

activities.title: The questions that decide the deal
